{{Short description|Polynomial interpolation using derivative values}}
In [[numerical analysis]], '''Hermite interpolation''', named after [[Charles Hermite]], is a method of [[polynomial interpolation]], which generalizes [[Lagrange interpolation]]. Lagrange interpolation allows computing a [[polynomial]] of [[degree of a polynomial|degree]] less than {{mvar|n}} that takes the same value at {{mvar|n}} given points as a given function. Instead, Hermite interpolation computes a polynomial of degree fewer than {{mvar|n}} such that the polynomial and its first few derivatives have the same values at {{mvar|m}} (fewer than {{mvar|n}}) given points as the given function and its first few derivatives at those points.  The number of pieces of information, function values and derivative values, must add up to <math>n</math>.

Hermite's method of interpolation is closely related to the [[Newton polynomial|Newton's interpolation method]], in that both can be derived from the calculation of [[divided differences]]. However, there are other methods for computing a Hermite interpolating polynomial. One can use [[linear algebra]], by taking the coefficients of the interpolating polynomial as [[unknown (mathematics)|unknowns]], and writing as [[linear equation]]s the constraints that the interpolating polynomial must satisfy. For another method, see {{slink||Using Chinese remainder theorem}}.  For yet another method, see {{slink||Using contour integration}}.

Hermite interpolating polynomials are also related to matrix [[generalized eigenspace]] projection via [[generalized Frobenius covariant]]s.

==Statement of the problem==

In a restricted formulation<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Traub |first1=J. F. |title=On Lagrange&mdash;Hermite interpolation |journal=Journal of the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics |date=December 1964 |volume=12 |issue=4 |pages=886&ndash;891 |doi=10.1137/0112076 |jstor=2946361 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2946361}}</ref>, Hermite interpolation consists,  given a [[differentiable function]], of computing a [[polynomial function]] of degree as low as possible such that the two functions and their first {{mvar|r}} derivatives take the same values at {{mvar|m}} different points. This means that one starts from {{tmath|1= n = m (r + 1)}} constraints, each resulting of one of the following given pairs of values:
<math display="block">\begin{matrix}
(x_1, y_1),       & (x_2, y_2),       & \ldots, & (x_m, y_m),  \\[1ex]
(x_1, y_1'),      & (x_2, y_2'),      & \ldots, & (x_m, y_m'), \\[1ex]
\vdots            & \vdots            &         & \vdots               \\[1.2ex]
(x_1, y_1^{(r)}), & (x_2, y_2^{(r)}), & \ldots, & (x_m, y_m^{(r)})
\end{matrix}</math>
As a polynomial of degree less than {{mvar|n}} is defined by {{mvar|n}} coefficients, the resulting polynomial must have a degree less than {{mvar|n}}, since, otherwise, the solution could not be unique. In a more general case, there is no need for {{mvar|r}} to have a fixed value; that is, some points may have more known derivatives than others. In this case the resulting polynomial has a degree less than the total number of constraints {{mvar|n}}.

Let us consider a polynomial {{tmath|h(x)}} of degree less than {{mvar|n}} with [[indeterminate (variable)|indeterminate]] coefficients; that is, the coefficients of {{tmath|h(x)}} are {{mvar|n}} new variables. Then, by writing the constraints that the interpolating polynomial must satisfy, one gets a [[system of linear equations|system of {{mvar|n}} linear equations]] in {{mvar|n}} unknowns.

Hermite used [[contour integration]] to prove that this is effectively the case here, and to find the unique solution, provided that the {{tmath|x_i}} are pairwise different.<ref name="Hermite1878">{{cite journal |last1=Hermite |first1=Charles |title=Sur la formule d'interpolation de Lagrange. |journal=Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik  |date=1878 |volume=84 |pages=70&ndash;79 |url=https://eudml.org/doc/148345}}</ref> Hermite interpolation is a problem of [[linear algebra]] that has the coefficients of the interpolation polynomial as unknown variables and a [[Vandermonde matrix#Confluent Vandermonde matrices|confluent Vandermonde matrix]] as its matrix.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Spitzbart |first1=A |title=A Generalization of Hermite Interpolation |journal=American Mathematical Monthly |date=January 1960 |volume=67 |issue=1 |pages=42&ndash;46 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1960.11989446 |jstor=2308924 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2308924 |access-date=2 June 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The general methods of linear algebra, and specific methods for confluent Vandermonde matrices are often used for computing the interpolation polynomial, as detailed in {{slink||Using linear algebra}}. Other methods are described below.

== Explicit formula ==
For a given set of {{mvar|m}} distinct nodes {{tmath|x_1, \dots, x_m}} with associated maximum derivative orders {{tmath|r_1, \dots, r_m}}, let {{tmath|1= n_i = r_i + 1}} be the multiplicity of node {{tmath|x_i}}, and let {{tmath|1=\textstyle n = \sum_{i=1}^m n_i}} be the total number of conditions. The Hermite interpolating polynomial {{tmath|h(x)}} is the unique polynomial of degree at most {{tmath|n - 1}} that satisfies the interpolation conditions:
<math display="block">h^{(j)}(x_i) = y_{i,j} \quad \text{for } i = 1, \dots, m \text{ and } j = 0, \dots, r_i.</math>

Define the complementary factor polynomial {{tmath|q_i(x)}} at node {{tmath|x_i}} as:
<math display="block">q_i(x) = \prod_{j \neq i} (x - x_j)^{n_j}.</math>

For each node {{tmath|x_i}}, let {{tmath|g_i(x)}} be the local {{tmath|r_i}}th degree [[Taylor polynomial]] matching the target derivative conditions:
<math display="block">g_i(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{r_i} \frac{y_{i,j}}{j!} (x - x_i)^j.</math>

The explicit closed-form formula for the Hermite interpolating polynomial {{tmath|h(x)}} is given by:
<math display="block">h(x) = \sum_{i=1}^m \underbrace{\left[ \sum_{j=0}^{r_i} \frac{1}{j!} \left. \left( \frac{g_i(\xi)}{q_i(\xi)} \right)^{(j)} \right|_{\xi = x_i} (x - x_i)^j \right]}_{\mathcal{T}_{x_i}^{m_i} \left[ g_i(x)/q_i(x) \right]} q_i(x),</math>
where {{tmath|\textstyle \mathcal{T}_{a}^{k} [f(x)]}} denotes the {{mvar|k}}th degree [[Taylor's theorem|Taylor operator]] of a function {{tmath|f(x)}} centered at {{tmath|1= x = a}}.

When {{tmath|1= r_i = 0}} for all distinct nodes {{tmath|x_i}}, meaning no derivative conditions are specified, this explicit closed-form formula reduces directly to the [[Lagrange polynomial#Definition|explicit formula of Lagrange polynomials]].

=== Interpolating a function in closed form ===
When interpolating a function {{tmath|f(x)}} that is {{tmath|r_i}} times differentiable at each node {{tmath|x_i}}, the interpolation conditions are determined by the function's derivatives (i.e., {{tmath|1=\textstyle y_{i,j} = f^{(j)}(x_i)}}). In this case, the local Taylor polynomial {{tmath|g_i(x)}} represents the {{tmath|r_i}}th degree Taylor expansion of {{tmath|f(x)}} at {{tmath|x_i}}.

Since the operator {{tmath|\textstyle \mathcal{T}_{x_i}^{r_i} }} isolates terms only up to order {{tmath|r_i}} at {{tmath|x_i}}, substituting {{tmath|f(x)}} in place of its local Taylor expansion {{tmath|g_i(x)}} yields the identical Taylor expansion up to order {{tmath|r_i}}:
<math display="block">\mathcal{T}_{x_i}^{r_i} \left[ \frac{g_i(x)}{q_i(x)} \right] = \mathcal{T}_{x_i}^{r_i} \left[ \frac{f(x)}{q_i(x)} \right].</math>

The explicit closed-form Hermite interpolating polynomial for {{tmath|f(x)}} can thus be expressed concisely as:
<math display="block">h(x) = \sum_{i=1}^m \mathcal{T}_{x_i}^{r_i} \left[ \frac{f(x)}{q_i(x)} \right] q_i(x).</math>

=== Basis polynomials in closed form ===
The Hermite interpolating polynomial {{tmath|h(x)}} can also be represented as a linear combination of Hermite basis polynomials {{tmath|h_{i,j}(x)}}:
<math display="block">h(x) = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=0}^{r_i} y_{i,j} h_{i,j}(x).</math>

An explicit closed-form expression for each basis polynomial {{tmath|h_{i,j}(x)}} can be obtained directly by choosing the local Taylor polynomial {{tmath|1=\textstyle g_i(x) = (x - x_i)^j / j!}} and setting {{tmath|1= g_k(x) = 0}} for all {{tmath|k \neq i}}. Substituting {{tmath|g_i(x)}} into the explicit formula yields:
<math display="block">h_{i,j}(x) = \mathcal{T}_{x_i}^{r_i} \left[ \frac{1}{j!} \frac{(x - x_i)^j}{q_i(x)} \right] q_i(x).</math>

Following the [[#Alternative basis construction via degree-0 basis polynomials|§ Alternative basis construction via degree-{{math|0}} basis polynomials]], the full set of basis polynomials can be constructed entirely using only the degree-{{math|0}} basis polynomial {{tmath|h_{i,0}(x)}}. For {{tmath|h_{i,0}(x)}}, the local Taylor polynomial simplifies to {{tmath|1= g_i(x) = 1}}, giving the explicit closed-form expression:
<math display="block">h_{i,0}(x) = \mathcal{T}_{x_i}^{r_i} \left[ \frac{1}{q_i(x)} \right] q_i(x).</math>

=== Proof of the closed form ===
The proof proceeds in three steps. First, it shows that evaluating derivatives at any node {{tmath|x_i}} isolates only the {{mvar|i}}th term in the summation. Next, it verifies that this term matches the required derivative values via local Taylor expansion. Finally, it establishes that the resulting polynomial satisfies the degree bound and uniqueness.

==== Vanishing of cross-terms at distinct nodes ====
Fix an arbitrary target node {{tmath|x_i}} and derivative order {{tmath|j \in \{0, \dots, r_i\} }}. Evaluating the {{mvar|j}}th derivative of {{tmath|h(x)}} at {{tmath|1= x = x_i}} yields:

<math display="block">h^{(j)}(x_i) = \left. \frac{d^j}{dx^j} \left( \sum_{k=1}^m \mathcal{T}_{x_k}^{r_k} \left[ \frac{g_k(x)}{q_k(x)} \right] q_k(x) \right) \right|_{x = x_i}</math>

For any node index {{tmath|k \neq i}}, the factor polynomial {{tmath|q_k(x)}} contains {{tmath|\textstyle (x - x_i)^{n_i} }} as an explicit factor:

<math display="block">q_k(x) = (x - x_i)^{n_i} \prod_{l \neq i, k} (x - x_l)^{n_l}</math>

By the general Leibniz rule, evaluating the {{mvar|j}}th derivative of {{tmath|\textstyle \mathcal{T}_{x_k}^{r_k} \left[ g_k(x) / q_k(x) \right] q_k(x)}} at {{tmath|1= x = x_i}} produces a linear combination of terms involving {{tmath|1=\textstyle \left. d^l\!\!/\!dx^l (x - x_i)^{n_i} \right\vert_{x = x_i} }} for {{tmath|0 \le l \le j}}. Because {{tmath|l \le j \le r_i < n_i}}, each derivative evaluates to {{math|0}} at {{tmath|1= x = x_i}}:

<math display="block">\left. \frac{d^l}{dx^l} (x - x_i)^{n_i} \right|_{x = x_i} = \left. \frac{n_i!}{(n_i - l)!} (x - x_i)^{n_i - l} \right|_{x = x_i} = 0 \quad \text{for all } 0 \le l \le j</math>

Consequently, all terms {{tmath|k \neq i}} in the summation vanish at {{tmath|1= x = x_i}}.

==== Verification of target interpolation conditions ====
Evaluating the remaining term {{tmath|1= k = i}} at {{tmath|1= x = x_i}}:

<math display="block">h^{(j)}(x_i) = \left. \frac{d^j}{dx^j} \left( \mathcal{T}_{x_i}^{r_i} \left[ \frac{g_i(x)}{q_i(x)} \right] q_i(x) \right) \right|_{x = x_i}</math>

Since the nodes are distinct, {{tmath|1=\textstyle q_i(x_i) = \prod_{k \neq i} (x_i - x_k)^{n_k} \neq 0}}, so the rational function {{tmath|g_i(x) / q_i(x)}} is analytic at {{tmath|1= x = x_i}}. By definition of the Taylor operator {{tmath|\textstyle \mathcal{T}_{x_i}^{r_i} }}, it expands locally around {{tmath|x_i}} as:

<math display="block">\mathcal{T}_{x_i}^{r_i} \left[ \frac{g_i(x)}{q_i(x)} \right] = \frac{g_i(x)}{q_i(x)} + O\bigl((x - x_i)^{n_i}\bigr)</math>

Multiplying by {{tmath|q_i(x)}} yields:

<math display="block">\mathcal{T}_{x_i}^{r_i} \left[ \frac{g_i(x)}{q_i(x)} \right] q_i(x) = \left( \frac{g_i(x)}{q_i(x)} + O\bigl((x - x_i)^{n_i}\bigr) \right) q_i(x) = g_i(x) + O\bigl((x - x_i)^{n_i}\bigr)</math>

Because the big {{mvar|O}} term represents an analytic function near {{tmath|x_i}} with a zero of order at least {{tmath|n_i}}, all of its derivatives of orders up to {{tmath|r_i}} vanish at {{tmath|1= x = x_i}}. Taking the {{mvar|j}}th derivative ({{tmath|0 \le j \le r_i}}) and evaluating at {{tmath|1= x = x_i}} yields:

<math display="block">h^{(j)}(x_i) = \left. \frac{d^j}{dx^j} \Bigl( g_i(x) + O\bigl((x - x_i)^{n_i}\bigr) \Bigr) \right|_{x = x_i} = g_i^{(j)}(x_i) + 0 = y_{i,j}</math>

Thus, {{tmath|h(x)}} satisfies all {{mvar|n}} interpolation conditions {{tmath|1=\textstyle h^{(j)}(x_i) = y_{i,j} }}.

==== Degree bound and uniqueness ====
For each distinct node {{tmath|x_i}}, the degree of {{tmath|\textstyle \mathcal{T}_{x_i}^{r_i} \left[ g_i(x) / q_i(x) \right]}} is at most {{tmath|r_i}}, and {{tmath|1=\textstyle \deg(q_i) = \sum_{j \neq i} n_j = n - n_i}}. Therefore, each term in {{tmath|h(x)}} has degree at most {{tmath|1= r_i + n - n_i = n - 1}}, so {{tmath|\deg(h) \le n - 1}}.

To establish uniqueness, assume another polynomial {{tmath|p(x)}} of degree {{tmath|\le n - 1}} satisfies the same {{mvar|n}} conditions. Because {{tmath|1=\textstyle h^{(j)}(x_i) = p^{(j)}(x_i) = y_{i,j} }} for all {{tmath|1 \le i \le m}} and {{tmath|0 \le j \le r_i}}, the difference {{tmath|1= d(x) = f(x) - p(x)}} satisfies {{tmath|1=\textstyle d^{(j)}(x_i) = 0}} for all {{tmath|0 \le j \le r_i}}, meaning each node {{tmath|x_i}} is a root of multiplicity at least {{tmath|n_i}}. This gives {{mvar|n}} roots counted with multiplicity across the {{mvar|m}} nodes. A nonzero polynomial of degree at most {{tmath|n - 1}} cannot have {{mvar|n}} roots counted with multiplicity. Therefore, {{tmath|f(x) - p(x)}} must be the zero polynomial, so {{tmath|1= f(x) = p(x)}}.

== Using Chinese remainder theorem ==
{{see also|Chinese remainder theorem#Hermite interpolation}}

Let {{mvar|m}} be a positive [[integer]] representing the number of distinct nodes, {{tmath|r_1, \ldots, r_m}} be nonnegative integers specifying the maximum derivative order at each node, {{tmath|1= n_i = r_i + 1}} be the multiplicity of node {{tmath|x_i}}, and the nodes {{tmath|x_1, \ldots, x_m}} be [[real number]]s or elements of any other [[field (mathematics)|field]] of [[characteristic of a field|characteristic]] zero. The Hermite interpolation problem consists of finding a [[polynomial]] {{tmath|h(x)}} such that 
<math display="block">h(x_i)=y_{i,0}, h'(x_i)=y_{i,1}, \ldots, h^{(r_i)}(x_i)=y_{i,r_i}</math>
for {{tmath|1= i=1,\ldots,m}}, where the {{tmath|y_{i,j} }} are given values in the same field as the {{tmath|x_i}}.

These conditions implies that the Taylor polynomial of {{tmath|h(x)}} of degree {{tmath|r_i}} at {{tmath|x_i}} is
<math display="block">g_i(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{r_i}\frac{y_{i,j}}{j!}(x-x_i)^j.</math>
In other words, the desired polynomial {{tmath|h(x)}} is [[modular arithmetic|congruent]] to this polynomial {{tmath|g_i(x)}} modulo {{tmath|1=\textstyle p_i(x) = (x-x_i)^{n_i} }}.

The [[Chinese remainder theorem#Over univariate polynomial rings and Euclidean domains|Chinese remainder theorem for polynomials]] implies that there is exactly one solution of degree less than {{tmath|1=\textstyle n=\sum_{i=1}^m n_i}}. 

Moreover, this solution can be computed with {{tmath|\textstyle O(n^2)}} arithmetic operations, or even faster with fast [[polynomial multiplication]].

This approach does not work in positive characteristic, because of the denominators of the coefficients of the Taylor polynomial. The approach through divided differences, [[#Using divided differences|below]], works in every characteristic.

=== Explicit construction via Chinese remainder theorem ===
For general Hermite interpolation, an explicit solution satisfying the system of simultaneous congruences can be constructed directly by following the [[Chinese_remainder_theorem#Existence_(constructive_proof)|constructive proof of the Chinese remainder theorem]].

The target polynomial {{tmath|h(x)}} must satisfy the system of modular equivalences:
<math display="block">h(x) \equiv g_i(x) \pmod{p_i(x)} \quad \text{for } i = 1, \dots, m,</math>
where {{tmath|1=\textstyle p_i(x) = (x - x_i)^{n_i} }} is the modulus polynomial at node {{tmath|x_i}}.

The solution is constructed iteratively by building a sequence of polynomials {{tmath|a_1(x), a_2(x), \dots, a_m(x)}} such that {{tmath|a_i(x)}} satisfies the first {{mvar|i}} congruences.

1. Base Step: Set the initial partial solution for {{tmath|1= i = 1}}:
<math display="block">a_1(x) = g_1(x).</math>

2. Inductive Step: Define {{tmath|1=\textstyle b_i(x) = \prod_{j=1}^i p_j(x)}} for {{tmath|1= i = 1, \dots, m}}. For {{tmath|1= i = 2, \dots, m}}, since {{tmath|b_{i-1}(x)}} and {{tmath|p_i(x)}} share no roots and thus are [[coprime polynomials|coprime]]. By [[Bézout's identity]], there exist polynomials {{tmath|u_i(x)}} and {{tmath|v_i(x)}} satisfying:
<math display="block">u_i(x) b_{i-1}(x) + v_i(x) p_i(x) = 1.</math>

The polynomials {{tmath|u_i(x)}} and {{tmath|v_i(x)}} can be solved together using the [[Extended_Euclidean_algorithm#Polynomial_extended_Euclidean_algorithm|polynomial extended Euclidean algorithm]].

Define the {{mvar|i}}th partial solution {{tmath|a_i(x)}} as:
<math display="block">a_i(x) = g_i(x) u_i(x) b_{i-1}(x) + a_{i-1}(x) v_i(x) p_i(x).</math>

This construction satisfies all conditions up to node {{mvar|i}}:
* Modulo {{tmath|p_i(x)}}, the term containing {{tmath|p_i(x)}} vanishes while {{tmath|u_i(x) b_{i-1}(x) \equiv 1 \pmod{p_i(x)} }}, giving {{tmath|a_i(x) \equiv g_i(x) \pmod{p_i(x)} }}.
* Modulo {{tmath|p_j(x)}} for any {{tmath|j < i}}, {{tmath|b_{i-1}(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{p_j(x)} }} and {{tmath|v_i(x) p_i(x) \equiv 1 \pmod{p_j(x)} }}, giving {{tmath|a_i(x) \equiv a_{i-1}(x) \equiv g_j(x) \pmod{p_j(x)} }}.

After {{tmath|m-1}} inductive steps, the final interpolating polynomial {{tmath|h(x)}} is obtained by reducing {{tmath|a_m(x)}} modulo the total degree product polynomial {{tmath|1=\textstyle b_m(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m p_i(x)}}:
<math display="block">h(x) = a_m(x) \bmod b_m(x).</math>

=== Basis polynomials via Chinese remainder theorem ===
Following [[#Alternative basis construction via degree-0 basis polynomials|§ Alternative basis construction via degree-{{math|0}} basis polynomials]], a full basis can be constructed by only solving the degree-{{math|0}} basis polynomials {{tmath|h_{i,0}(x)}}, which can be obtained in a simplified manner.

For each node {{tmath|x_i}}, the degree-{{math|0}} basis polynomial {{tmath|h_{i,0}(x)}} must satisfy:
* {{tmath|h_{i,0}(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{p_j(x)} \quad \text{for } j \neq i}},
* {{tmath|h_{i,0}(x) \equiv 1 \pmod{p_i(x)} }}.

To satisfy the zero-remainder conditions at all other nodes {{tmath|j \neq i}}, {{tmath|h_{i,0}(x)}} must contain the product factor {{tmath|1=\textstyle q_i(x) = \prod_{j \neq i} p_j(x)}}. Thus, {{tmath|1= h_{i,0}(x) = u_i(x) q_i(x)}} for some polynomial {{tmath|u_i(x)}}.

Since {{tmath|p_i(x)}} and {{tmath|q_i(x)}} share no roots and thus are coprime, Bézout's identity guarantees the existence of polynomials {{tmath|u_i(x)}} and {{tmath|v_i(x)}} satisfying:
<math display="block">u_i(x) q_i(x) + v_i(x) p_i(x) = 1.</math>

Taking this relation modulo {{tmath|p_i(x)}}, the term {{tmath|v_i(x) p_i(x)}} vanishes, showing that {{tmath|u_i(x)}} is a modular multiplicative inverse of {{tmath|q_i(x)}}:
<math display="block">u_i(x) q_i(x) \equiv 1 \pmod{p_i(x)}.</math>

Since the polynomial {{tmath|v_i(x)}} is not required for the construction, {{tmath|u_i(x)}} can be computed directly using [[Extended_Euclidean_algorithm#Computing_multiplicative_inverses_in_modular_structures|half extended Euclidean algorithm]] that tracks only one set of Bézout coefficients.

Because the degree of the modular inverse {{tmath|u_i(x)}} obtained via the extended Euclidean algorithm is strictly less than {{tmath|1= \deg(p_i) = n_i}}, and {{tmath|1= \deg(q_i) = n - n_i}}, the product degree is bounded by:
<math display="block">\deg(u_i q_i) = \deg(u_i) + \deg(q_i) < n_i + (n - n_i) = n.</math>
Thus, {{tmath|\deg(u_i q_i) \le n - 1}}, meaning the product {{tmath|u_i(x) q_i(x)}} already satisfies the degree constraint without requiring any further modular reduction, yielding directly the unique degree-{{math|0}} basis polynomial {{tmath|1= h_{i,0}(x) = u_i(x) q_i(x)}}.

For any individual simple node {{tmath|x_i}} with no derivative conditions ({{tmath|1= r_i = 0}}), {{tmath|1= p_i(x) = x - x_i}}. By the [[polynomial remainder theorem]], the modular condition {{tmath|u_i(x) q_i(x) \equiv 1 \pmod{x - x_i} }} simplifies to the point evaluation {{tmath|1= u_i(x_i) q_i(x_i) = 1}}. In this case, {{tmath|u_i(x)}} reduces to a scalar constant that can be evaluated directly in closed form:
<math display="block">u_i(x) = \frac{1}{q_i(x_i)} = \prod_{j \neq i} \frac{1}{p_j(x_i)}.</math>

== Using divided differences ==
{{see also|Divided differences|Newton polynomial}}
For a given set of {{mvar|m}} distinct nodes {{tmath|x_1, \dots, x_m}} with associated maximum derivative orders {{tmath|r_1, \dots, r_m}}, let {{tmath|1= n_i = r_i + 1}} be the multiplicity of node {{tmath|x_i}}, and let {{tmath|1=\textstyle n = \sum_{i=1}^m n_i}} be the total number of conditions. An efficient way to construct the Hermite interpolating polynomial {{tmath|h(x)}} is by extending [[Newton polynomial|Newton's divided difference method]]. Since Newton interpolation and Lagrange interpolation construct the exact same unique polynomial for a distinct set of nodes, Newton's method can be generalized to the confluent case where distinct nodes coalesce via [[confluent divided differences]]. To interpolate a function {{tmath|f(x)}} or a given set of derivative conditions {{tmath|y_{i,j} }} (for {{tmath|1= i = 1, \dots, m}} and {{tmath|1= j = 0, \dots, r_i}}), the original set of nodes is transformed into a dataset {{tmath|z_1, \dots, z_n}} by repeating each node {{tmath|x_i}} according to its multiplicity {{tmath|n_i}} times:
<math display="block">(z_1, \dots, z_n) = (\underbrace{x_1, \dots, x_1}_{n_1 \text{ times}}, \underbrace{x_2, \dots, x_2}_{n_2 \text{ times}}, \dots, \underbrace{x_m, \dots, x_m}_{n_m \text{ times}}).</math>
When constructing the [[Divided differences|divided difference table]] for this dataset, the standard finite difference quotient for identical confluent nodes would result in an undefined {{tmath|0/0}} expression; these entries are directly replaced by the corresponding scaled derivative values {{tmath|\textstyle f^{(j)}(x_i)/j!}} (or {{tmath|y_{i,j}/j!}}). The interpolating polynomial is then represented in Newton form:
<math display="block">h(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n f[z_1, \dots, z_i] \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (x - z_j).</math>
Once the target function and derivative values are known, this generalized construction requires only basic algebraic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division) to compute the divided difference table and construct the polynomial.

Through [[Divided differences#Cauchy's integral formula|Cauchy's integral formula for confluent divided differences]], constructing the Hermite interpolating polynomial via divided differences can also be viewed as a contour integration approach, providing an alternative formulation to the integral representation described in {{slink||Using contour integral}}.

=== Simple case with only first derivatives ===
{{Anchor|1=Simple case when all k=2}} <!--old subsection name-->
Here we will consider only the simplest case {{tmath|1= r_i = 1}} (i.e., {{tmath|1= n_i = 2}}) for all distinct nodes. Therefore, given {{mvar|m}} distinct nodes {{tmath|x_1, \ldots, x_m}}, and values {{tmath|f(x_1), \ldots, f(x_m)}} and {{tmath|f'(x_1), \ldots, f'(x_m)}} for a function {{tmath|f(x)}} that we want to interpolate, we create a new dataset {{tmath|z_1, \ldots, z_{2m} }} such that
<math display="block">z_{2i-1} = z_{2i} = x_i.</math>

Now, we create a divided differences table for the nodes {{tmath|z_1, \ldots, z_{2m} }}. However, for some divided differences,
<math display="block">z_i = z_{i + 1}
\implies f[z_i, z_{i+1}] = \frac{f(z_{i+1})-f(z_{i})}{z_{i+1}-z_{i}} = \frac{0}{0}</math>
which is undefined.
In this case, the divided difference is replaced by {{tmath|f'(z_i)}}. All others are calculated normally.

=== General case for higher-order derivatives ===
{{Anchor|A more general case when k&gt;2}} <!--old subsection name-->
In the general case, suppose a given node {{tmath|x_i}} has up to {{tmath|r_i}}th order derivatives. Then the dataset {{tmath|z_1, \ldots, z_n}} contains {{tmath|n_i}} adjacent identical copies of {{tmath|x_i}}. When creating the table, divided differences of {{tmath|j + 1}} (for {{tmath|1= j = 0, \ldots, r_i}}) identical values will be calculated as
<math display="block">f[\underbrace{x_i, \ldots, x_i}_{j + 1 \,\text{times}}]=\frac{f^{(j)}(x_i)}{j!}.</math>

For example,
<math display="block">f[x_i, x_i, x_i]=\frac{f''(x_i)}{2}</math>
<math display="block">f[x_i, x_i, x_i, x_i]=\frac{f^{(3)}(x_i)}{6}</math>
etc.

A fast algorithm for the fully general case is given by Schneider and Werner.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Schneider |first1=C |last2=Werner |first2=W |title=Hermite Interpolation: The Barycentric Approach |journal=Computing |date=1991 |volume=46 |pages=35&ndash;51 |doi=10.1007/BF02239010 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02239010|url-access=subscription }}</ref>  A slower but more numerically  stable algorithm is given by Corless and Fillion.<ref name="CF2013">{{cite book |last1=Corless |first1=Robert M |last2=Fillion |first2=Nicolas |title=A Graduate Introduction to Numerical Methods |date=2013 |publisher=Springer |location=New York |isbn=978-1-4614-8452-3 }}</ref>

=== Example ===

==== Case of uniform derivative orders ====
Consider the function {{tmath|1=\textstyle f(x) = x^8 + 1}}. Evaluating the function and its first two derivatives at {{tmath|x \in \{-1, 0, 1\} }}, we obtain the following data:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: right; padding: 1em; margin-left: 1.5em"
|-
! {{tmath|x}}  || {{tmath|f(x)}} || {{tmath|f'(x)}}  || {{tmath|f''(x)}}
|-
| {{math|−1}} ||  {{math|2}}   ||  {{math|−8}}   || {{math|56}}
|-
| {{math|0}}  ||  {{math|1}}   ||  {{math|0}}    || {{math|0}}
|-
| {{math|1}}  ||  {{math|2}}   ||  {{math|8}}    || {{math|56}}
|}

Since we have two derivatives to work with, we construct the dataset
<math display="block">(z_i, \ldots, z_n) = (-1, -1, -1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1).</math>
Our divided difference table is then:
<math display="block">
\begin{array}{llcclrrrrr}
z_1 = -1  &  f[z_1] = 2  &                          &                         &                           &      &     &   &    & \\
          &              &  \frac{f'(z_1)}{1} = -8  &                         &                           &      &     &   &    & \\
z_2 = -1  &  f[z_2] = 2  &                          & \frac{f''(z_2)}{2} = 28 &                           &      &     &   &    & \\
          &              &  \frac{f'(z_2)}{1} = -8  &                         &  f[z_4,z_3,z_2,z_1] = -21 &      &     &   &    & \\
z_3 = -1  &  f[z_3] = 2  &                          & f[z_4,z_3,z_2] = 7      &                           &  15  &     &   &    & \\
          &              &  f[z_4,z_3] = -1         &                         &  f[z_5,z_4,z_3,z_2] = -6  &      & -10 &   &    & \\
z_4 =  0  &  f[z_4] = 1  &                          & f[z_5,z_4,z_3] = 1      &                           &   5  &     & 4 &    & \\
          &              &  \frac{f'(z_4)}{1} = 0   &                         &  f[z_6,z_5,z_4,z_3] = -1  &      &  -2 &   & -1 & \\
z_5 =  0  &  f[z_5] = 1  &                          & \frac{f''(z_5)}{2} = 0  &                           &   1  &     & 2 &    & 1 \\
          &              &  \frac{f'(z_5)}{1} = 0   &                         &  f[z_7,z_6,z_5,z_4] =  1  &      &   2 &   &  1 & \\
z_6 =  0  &  f[z_6] = 1  &                          & f[z_7,z_6,z_5] = 1      &                           &   5  &     & 4 &    & \\
          &              &  f[z_7,z_6] = 1          &                         &  f[z_8,z_7,z_6,z_5] =  6  &      &  10 &   &    & \\
z_7 =  1  &  f[z_7] = 2  &                          & f[z_8,z_7,z_6] = 7      &                           &  15  &     &   &    & \\
          &              &  \frac{f'(z_7)}{1} = 8   &                         &  f[z_9,z_8,z_7,z_6] =  21 &      &     &   &    & \\
z_8 =  1  &  f[z_8] = 2  &                          & \frac{f''(z_8)}{2} = 28 &                           &      &     &   &    & \\
          &              &  \frac{f'(z_8)}{1} = 8   &                         &                           &      &     &   &    & \\
z_9 =  1  &  f[z_9] = 2  &                          &                         &                           &      &     &   &    & \\
\end{array}
</math>
and by taking the coefficients from the diagonal of the divided difference table, and multiplying the {{mvar|i}}th coefficient by {{tmath|1=\textstyle \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (x - z_j)}}, as we would when constructing Newton form to generate a Newton polynomial, the generated polynomial {{tmath|h(x)}} is
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
h(x) &= 2 - 8(x+1) + 28(x+1) ^2 - 21 (x+1)^3 + 15x(x+1)^3 - 10x^2(x+1)^3 \\
&\quad{} + 4x^3(x+1)^3 -1x^3(x+1)^3(x-1)+x^3(x+1)^3(x-1)^2 \\
&=2 - 8 + 28 - 21 - 8x + 56x - 63x + 15x + 28x^2 - 63x^2 + 45x^2 - 10x^2 - 21x^3 \\
&\quad {}+ 45x^3 - 30x^3 + 4x^3 + x^3 + x^3 + 15x^4 - 30x^4 + 12x^4 + 2x^4 + x^4 \\
&\quad {}- 10x^5 + 12x^5 - 2x^5 + 4x^5 - 2x^5 - 2x^5 - x^6 + x^6 - x^7 + x^7 + x^8 \\
&= x^8 + 1.
\end{align}
</math>

==== Case of non-uniform derivative orders ====
Consider the following set of derivative conditions {{tmath|y_{i,j} }} at nodes {{tmath|x_i \in \{-1, 0, 1\} }}:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: right; padding: 1em; margin-left: 1.5em"
|-
!  {{tmath|i}}  ||  {{tmath|x_i}}  ||  {{tmath|y_{i,0} }}  ||  {{tmath|y_{i,1} }}
|-
|  {{math|1}}   ||  {{math|−1}}    ||  {{math|1}}          ||  {{math|2}}
|-
|  {{math|2}}   ||  {{math|0}}     ||  {{math|1}}          ||
|-
|  {{math|3}}   ||  {{math|1}}     ||  {{math|-1}}         ||  {{math|-2}}
|}

For this example with non-uniform derivative orders, we construct the dataset
<math display="block">(z_1,\ldots,z_n) = (-1,-1,0,1,1).</math>
Denoting the divided differences as {{tmath|y[z_a, \dots, z_b]}} when constructed from the derivative conditions {{tmath|y_{i,j} }}, the constructed divided difference table is given by:
<math display="block">
\begin{array}{llclrr}
z_1 = -1  &  y[z_1] = y_{1,0} = 1   &                             &                       &               &     \\
          &                         &  \frac{y_{1,1}}{1} = 2      &                       &               &     \\
z_2 = -1  &  y[z_2] = y_{1,0} = 1   &                             &  y[z_3,z_2,z_1] = -2  &               &     \\
          &                         &  y[z_3,z_2] = \phantom{-}0  &                       &  \frac{1}{2}  &     \\
z_3 = 0   &  y[z_3] = y_{2,0} = 1   &                             &  y[z_4,z_3,z_2] = -1  &               &  0  \\
          &                         &  y[z_4,z_3] = -2            &                       &  \frac{1}{2}  &     \\
z_4 = 1   &  y[z_4] = y_{3,0} = -1  &                             &  y[z_5,z_4,z_3] = 0   &               &     \\
          &                         &  \frac{y_{3,1}}{1} = -2     &                       &               &     \\
z_5 = 1   &  y[z_5] = y_{3,0} = -1  &                             &                       &               &     \\
\end{array}
</math>
and the generated polynomial {{tmath|h(x)}} in Newton form is
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
h(x) &= 1 + 2(x+1) - 2(x+1)^2 + \frac{1}{2}x(x+1)^2 + 0x(x+1)^2(x-1) \\
&= \frac{1}{2}x^3 - x^2 - \frac{3}{2}x + 1.
\end{align}
</math>

== Using linear algebra ==
{{Anchor|A perspective from linear algebra}} <!--old subsection name-->
{{see also|Vandermonde matrix#Confluent Vandermonde matrices|Lagrange polynomial#A perspective from linear algebra}}

The interpolation problem can also be formulated and solved directly using linear algebra in a similar way to Lagrange interpolation, by replacing the standard Vandermonde matrix with a confluent Vandermonde matrix to account for both function values and derivative conditions at each node.

Let {{mvar|m}} be the number of distinct nodes {{tmath|x_1, \ldots, x_m}}, let {{tmath|n_i}} be the multiplicity of node {{tmath|x_i}} representing the number of specified values including derivatives, and let {{tmath|1=\textstyle n = \sum_{i=1}^m n_i}} be the total number of data conditions. Let {{tmath|\mathbf V}} be the constructed confluent Vandermonde matrix, let {{tmath|1=\textstyle \mathbf H = \mathbf V^{-1} }} be its inverse, and let {{tmath|1= d = n - 1}} be the degree bound of the interpolating polynomial. The matrix {{tmath|\mathbf H}} is given by:
<math display="block">\mathbf H = \begin{pmatrix} H_{00} & \cdots & H_{0d} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ H_{d0} & \cdots & H_{dd} \end{pmatrix}.</math>

The sample vector {{tmath|\mathbf{y} }} stacks all target function values and derivative constraints into a single column vector of total dimension {{mvar|n}}. The pair of node index {{mvar|i}} and derivative index {{mvar|j}} is mapped to a single flattened index {{tmath|k \in \{0, \dots, d\} }} via the indexing function:
<math display="block">k = \sigma(i, j) = j + \sum_{l=1}^{i-1} n_l.</math>

Given the interpolation condition vector {{tmath|\mathbf{y} }}, the coefficient vector {{tmath|1=\textstyle \mathbf{a} = \begin{pmatrix} a_0 & a_1 & \cdots & a_d \end{pmatrix}^T}} of the Hermite interpolating polynomial {{tmath|1=\textstyle h(x) = \sum_{k=0}^d a_k x^k}} can be computed as:
<math display="block">\mathbf{a} = \mathbf H \mathbf{y}.</math>

Furthermore, the individual Hermite interpolating basis polynomials {{tmath|h_{i,j}(x)}} correspond to the basis polynomials {{tmath|h_k(x)}} in the flattened indexing under {{tmath|1= k = \sigma(i,j)}}, allowing the interpolating polynomial to be expressed equivalently as:
<math display="block">h(x) = \sum_{k=0}^d y_k h_k(x) = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=0}^{n_i-1} y_{\sigma(i,j)} h_{i,j}(x).</math>
The basis polynomials {{tmath|1= h_{i,j}(x) = h_k(x)}} can be constructed directly from the columns of {{tmath|\mathbf H}}:
<math display="block">h_{i,j}(x) = h_k(x) = H_{0k} + H_{1k} x + \cdots + H_{dk} x^d.</math>

In numerical practice, directly computing {{tmath|\mathbf H}} by inverting the confluent Vandermonde matrix is generally avoided because confluent Vandermonde matrices are notoriously [[ill-conditioned]]. As the number of nodes or their degree increases, their condition number grows exponentially, making direct matrix inversion numerically unstable and highly sensitive to floating-point errors.

== Using contour integration ==
An elegant representation and derivation of the Hermite interpolating polynomial can be obtained using contour integration in the [[complex plane]], a formulation originally introduced by Charles Hermite in 1878.<ref name="Hermite1878"/>

Let {{mvar|m}} be the number of distinct interpolation nodes {{tmath|x_1, \dots, x_m}}, with corresponding multiplicities {{tmath|n_1, \dots, n_m}}. The total number of interpolation conditions is {{tmath|1=\textstyle n = \sum_{i=1}^m n_i}}. Define the product polynomial of all node factors as
<math display="block">q(x) = \prod_{i=1}^m (x-x_i)^{n_i}.</math>

Suppose the target function {{mvar|f}} is [[holomorphic function|analytic]] inside and on a positively oriented simple closed contour {{tmath|\Gamma}} in the complex plane that encloses the evaluation point {{tmath|x}} as well as all nodes {{tmath|x_i}}. The Hermite interpolating polynomial {{tmath|h(x)}} of degree at most {{tmath|n-1}} can be expressed as
<math display="block">h(x) = f(x) - \frac{q(x)}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma} \frac{f(\zeta)}{q(\zeta)(\zeta-x)} \, d\zeta.</math>

Alternatively, by expressing {{tmath|f(x)}} via [[Cauchy's integral formula]] as
<math display="block">f(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma} \frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta-x} \, d\zeta</math>
and absorbing it into the integral, {{tmath|h(x)}} can be written equivalently as
<math display="block">h(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma} \frac{f(\zeta)\left(q(\zeta)-q(x)\right)}{q(\zeta)(\zeta-x)} \, d\zeta.</math>

=== Derivation using residues ===
Consider the [[meromorphic function]]
<math display="block">F(\zeta) = \frac{f(\zeta)}{q(\zeta)(\zeta-x)}.</math>

Assuming {{tmath|x}} is not one of the nodes {{tmath|x_i}}, {{tmath|F(\zeta)}} has the following poles inside {{tmath|\Gamma}}:
* A [[simple pole]] at {{tmath|1= \zeta = x}}.
* Poles at {{tmath|1= \zeta = x_i}} with order {{tmath|n_i}} for each {{tmath|1= i = 1, \dots, m}}.

By the [[residue theorem]], integrating {{tmath|F(\zeta)}} along {{tmath|\Gamma}} yields
<math display="block">\frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma} \frac{f(\zeta)}{q(\zeta)(\zeta-x)} \, d\zeta = \operatorname{Res}_{\zeta=x} F(\zeta) + \sum_{i=1}^m \operatorname{Res}_{\zeta=x_i} F(\zeta).</math>

The residue at the simple pole {{tmath|1= \zeta = x}} is easily evaluated as
<math display="block">\operatorname{Res}_{\zeta=x} F(\zeta) = \lim_{\zeta \to x} \, (\zeta - x) \frac{f(\zeta)}{q(\zeta)(\zeta-x)} = \frac{f(x)}{q(x)}.</math>

Substituting this residue back into the integral equation gives
<math display="block">\frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma} \frac{f(\zeta)}{q(\zeta)(\zeta-x)} \, d\zeta = \frac{f(x)}{q(x)} + \sum_{i=1}^m \operatorname{Res}_{\zeta=x_i} F(\zeta).</math>

Rearranging terms to isolate {{tmath|f(x)}} gives
<math display="block">f(x) = \frac{q(x)}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma} \frac{f(\zeta)}{q(\zeta)(\zeta-x)} \, d\zeta - q(x) \sum_{i=1}^m \operatorname{Res}_{\zeta=x_i} F(\zeta).</math>

Each residue {{tmath|1= \operatorname{Res}_{\zeta=x_i} F(\zeta)}} is a [[rational function]] in {{tmath|x}} whose denominator factors are cancelled out by {{tmath|q(x)}}. Summing these terms yields a polynomial in {{tmath|x}} of degree at most {{tmath|n-1}} that satisfies all interpolation conditions. Thus, it corresponds precisely to the Hermite interpolating polynomial {{tmath|h(x)}}:
<math display="block">h(x) = -q(x) \sum_{i=1}^m \operatorname{Res}_{\zeta=x_i} F(\zeta).</math>
Substituting this definition into the expression for {{tmath|f(x)}} and rearrange yields
<math display="block">h(x) = f(x) - \frac{q(x)}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma} \frac{f(\zeta)}{q(\zeta)(\zeta-x)} \, d\zeta.</math>

Consequently, the interpolation error {{tmath|f(x) - h(x)}} (see also {{slink||Error}}) is given directly by the integral term:
<math display="block">f(x) - h(x) = \frac{q(x)}{2\pi i} \oint_{\Gamma} \frac{f(\zeta)}{q(\zeta)(\zeta-x)} \, d\zeta.</math>

== Common low-degree cases ==

=== Cubic Hermite spline ===
{{Main|Cubic Hermite spline}}
Cubic Hermite splines are widely used in numerical analysis, computer graphics, and motion planning for keyframe animation, path trajectories, and geometric modeling because they ensure smooth {{tmath|\textstyle C^1}} continuity while providing precise local control over both endpoint positions and tangents.

On the unit interval {{tmath|x \in [0, 1]}}, the two endpoints are defined as {{tmath|1= x_1 = 0}} and {{tmath|1= x_2 = 1}}, the cubic Hermite interpolant {{tmath|h(x)}} is uniquely determined by boundary values and first derivatives {{tmath|f(0), f(1), f'(0), f'(1)}}:
<math display="block">h(x) = f(0) h_{1,0}(x) + f'(0) h_{1,1}(x) + f(1) h_{2,0}(x) + f'(1) h_{2,1}(x)</math>

where the four basis polynomials are:
<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
h_{1,0}(x) &= 2x^3 - 3x^2 + 1, \\
h_{1,1}(x) &= x^3 - 2x^2 + x, \\
h_{2,0}(x) &= -2x^3 + 3x^2, \\
h_{2,1}(x) &= x^3 - x^2.
\end{aligned}</math>

For rescaling to arbitrary intervals, piecewise multi-interval construction, or extension to 2D/3D parametric curves, see [[Cubic Hermite spline#Interpolation on an arbitrary interval|Cubic Hermite spline]].

=== Quintic Hermite interpolation ===
The quintic Hermite interpolation based on the function {{tmath|f(x)}}, its first {{tmath|f'(x)}} and second derivatives {{tmath|f''(x)}} at two different points ({{tmath|x_1}} and {{tmath|x_2}}) can be used for example to interpolate the position of an object based on its position, velocity and acceleration.
The general form is given by
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
      f(x) & = f(x_1) + f'(x_1) (x - x_1) + \frac{1}{2}f''(x_1) (x - x_1)^2 + \frac{f(x_2) - y(x_1) - f'(x_1) (x_2 - x_1) - \frac{1}{2} f''(x_1) (x_2 - x_1)^2}{(x_2 - x_1)^3} (x - x_1)^3 \\
           & + \frac{3 f(x_1) - 3 f(x_2) + 2\left( f'(x_1) + \frac{1}{2}f'(x_2) \right) (x_2 - x_1) + \frac{1}{2}  f''(x_1) (x_2 - x_1)^2}{(x_2 - x_1)^4} (x - x_1)^3 (x - x_2) \\
           & + \frac{6 f(x_2) - 6 f(x_1) - 3 \left( f'(x_1) + f'(x_2) \right) (x_2 - x_1) + \frac{1}{2}\left( f''(x_2) - f''(x_1) \right) (x_2 - x_1)^2}{(x_2 - x_1)^5} (x - x_1)^3 (x - x_2)^2.
\end{align}
</math>

== Basis polynomials ==
For a given set of {{mvar|m}} distinct nodes {{tmath|x_1, \dots, x_m}} with associated maximum derivative orders {{tmath|r_1, \dots, r_m}}, let {{tmath|1= n_i = r_i + 1}} be the multiplicity of node {{tmath|x_i}}, and let {{tmath|1=\textstyle n = \sum_i n_i}} be the total number of conditions. The Hermite interpolating polynomial {{tmath|h(x)}} can be expressed as a linear combination of basis polynomials {{tmath|h_{i,j}(x)}}:
<math display="block">h(x) = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=0}^{r_i} y_{i,j} h_{i,j}(x),</math>
where each basis polynomial {{tmath|h_{i,j}(x)}} is uniquely defined as the interpolating polynomial of degree at most {{tmath|n - 1}} for the basis conditions given by the [[Kronecker delta]]:
<math display="block">\left. \frac{d^l}{dx^l} h_{i,j}(x) \right|_{x = x_k} = \delta_{i,k} \delta_{j,l} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } k = i \text{ and } l = j, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}</math>

To construct a specific basis polynomial {{tmath|h_{i, j}(x)}} using general methods for solving Hermite interpolation (such as those described in this article), one specifies a system of target conditions {{tmath|\textstyle y_{k, l}^{(i, j)} }} across all nodes {{tmath|x_k}} and derivative orders {{tmath|0 \le l \le r_k}}:
<math display="block">y_{k, l}^{(i, j)} = \delta_{i,k} \delta_{j,l} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } k = i \text{ and } l = j, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}</math>

By passing these target conditions {{tmath|\textstyle y_{k, l}^{(i, j)} }} as input values into any general method for solving Hermite interpolation, the resulting unique interpolating polynomial generated by the method is precisely the basis polynomial {{tmath|h_{i, j}(x)}}. Repeating this process for each pair of indices {{tmath|(i, j)}} constructs the full set of {{mvar|n}} basis polynomials.

=== Alternative basis construction via degree-0 basis polynomials ===
Let {{tmath|1=\textstyle q(x) = \prod_i (x - x_i)^{n_i} }} be the polynomial of degree {{mvar|n}}, which vanishes at each node {{tmath|x_i}} with multiplicity {{tmath|n_i}}. Once the degree-{{math|0}} basis polynomials {{tmath|h_{i,0}(x)}} (corresponding to the function value condition {{tmath|1= y_{i,0} = 1}} at node {{tmath|x_i}}) are obtained, the higher-order derivative basis polynomials {{tmath|h_{i,j}(x)}} for {{tmath|1 \le j \le r_i}} can be constructed directly via polynomial reduction:
<math display="block">h_{i,j}(x) = \left( \frac{(x - x_i)^j}{j!} h_{i,0}(x) \right) \bmod q(x).</math>

Taking the remainder modulo {{tmath|q(x)}} guarantees that {{tmath|1= \deg(h_{i,j}) < \deg(q) = n}}, projecting the polynomial into the subspace of degree at most {{tmath|n - 1}}. Because {{tmath|q(x)}} vanishes at every node {{tmath|x_i}} to order {{tmath|n_i}}, all target derivative evaluation conditions at the nodes are preserved under this modular reduction. This bounds the degree and ensures that each constructed {{tmath|h_{i,j}(x)}} is the unique polynomial of degree at most {{tmath|n - 1}} satisfying its corresponding interpolation conditions.

This construction is particularly advantageous when direct evaluation of higher-order basis polynomials {{tmath|h_{i,j}(x)}} is computationally expensive or numerically unstable. In some cases, the degree-{{math|0}} basis polynomials {{tmath|h_{i,0}(x)}} are simply cleaner and easier to construct and compute, allowing all remaining derivative basis polynomials for that node to be generated efficiently through straightforward polynomial multiplication and modular reduction.

==Error==
Let {{mvar|m}} be the number of distinct nodes {{tmath|x_1, \ldots, x_m}}, let {{tmath|n_i}} be the multiplicity of node {{tmath|x_i}} representing the number of specified values including derivatives, and let {{tmath|1=\textstyle n = \sum_{i=1}^m n_i}} be the total number of interpolation conditions. Denote the constructed Hermite interpolating polynomial as {{tmath|h(x)}} and the original function as {{tmath|f(x)}}. Consider first the real-valued case. Let {{tmath|1=\textstyle a = \min_i x_i}} and {{tmath|1=\textstyle b = \max_i x_i}}. Evaluating at a point {{tmath|x \in [a, b]}}, the error function is
<math display="block">f(x) - h(x) = \frac{f^{(n)}(c)}{n!} \prod_{i=1}^m (x - x_i)^{n_i},</math>
where {{mvar|c}} is an unknown value within the range {{tmath|[a, b]}}, derived using a generalization of the [[Mean value theorem (divided differences)|mean value theorem for divided differences]] to confluent nodes.
The degree of the product polynomial on the right is {{mvar|n}}, which is one higher than the degree bound {{tmath|n - 1}} for {{tmath|h(x)}}. Furthermore, the error and all its derivatives up to order {{tmath|n_i - 1}} are zero at each node {{tmath|x_i}}, as expected.

In the complex case, as described for example on p. 360 in <ref name=CF2013 />,
<math display="block">f(z) - h(z) = \frac{q(z)}{2\pi i} \oint_C \frac{f(\zeta)}{q(\zeta)(\zeta-z)}d\zeta</math>
where the contour {{mvar|C}} encloses {{mvar|z}} and all the nodes {{tmath|x_i}}, and {{tmath|1=\textstyle q(z) = \prod_{i=1}^m (z - x_i)^{n_i} }} is the product polynomial of all node factors.
